Lose consciousness? Pass out? No, I don't think so. I mean, I remember the whole thing pretty clearly. Well, as clearly as you can remember being strapped to a stretcher while a bunch of paramedics are shouting at each other. They were making such a racket, you'd think they were trying to wake the dead. And the siren! No, no, I never blacked out or lost consciousness or anything like that. Not even for a second. I was wide awake the whole time, watching the whole circus happen. Like I said, I remember the ambulance ride, I remember the squeaky cart, all of it. 

I actually remember looking out the back window of the ambulance and seeing Mrs. Gable's house as we went past. She lives on the corner of Elm and Maple. She's got these huge hydrangeas in her front yard, beautiful blue ones. She told my wife her secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil to make it acidic. We tried it last spring, saved all our Folgers grounds in a plastic tub under the sink. But our dog, Buster—he's a beagle mix, nose gets him into all sorts of trouble—he got into the tub and ate half the coffee grounds. I had to call the emergency vet at ten o'clock at night. Cost me two hundred dollars just for them to tell me he was gonna be jittery for a day and to make sure he drank water. He was practically vibrating, running laps around the coffee table until 3 AM. 

But no, I didn't pass out or black out at all with the heart thing. I was awake for the whole ordeal.

Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a bit here! No, they never said cardiac arrest. It didn't stop beating, and it definitely didn't quit working. If my heart completely quit working, I'm pretty sure I wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you right now.

No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I talk plenty, you can probably tell that. My wife says I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. No, no, they didn't say anything like that. No stopping, no... whatever that other word you just said was. Ventricular something. The old Maytag finally gave up the ghost. Sounded like a jet engine taking off in the basement every time it hit the spin cycle. My wife made me go to Sears to look at new ones, but Sears is closed now, isn't it? We ended up at Home Depot. The guy there—wearing an orange apron, name tag said 'Kevin'—tried to sell us one of those smart washers that connects to the Wi-Fi. I said, \"Kevin, why on earth does my washing machine need the internet? Is it going to email me when the socks are clean?\" It's ridiculous. Everything has to have a computer in it now. Even my toaster has a digital screen. It's a toaster! You push the lever down, the bread gets hot. You don't need a microchip for that. \n\nBut anyway, no, they didn't say my heart stopped or went into a crazy rhythm. Just a scare, like I said.\n\nDoctor: When you had that cardiac scare, did the doctors ever tell you that your heart completely stopped beating, or that you weren't getting enough oxygen and your brain wasn't getting blood flow for a period of time?\n\nPatient: No, they never said anything like that. They didn't say it stopped completely, and nobody mentioned anything about my brain not getting blood or oxygen or whatever. It felt like they were trying to drain me dry. This one nurse, she came in at three in the morning—three in the morning!—just to take more blood. She had this little cart that squeaked every time the wheels turned. Squeak, squeak, squeak, all the way down the hall. You'd think a hospital would have some WD-40 lying around. I keep a can of it in the garage, right next to my fishing tackle. I haven't been fishing in ages, though. The lake's gotten so crowded lately, all these speedboats zipping around, scaring the bass away. You can't even enjoy a quiet morning out on the water anymore without some guy on a jet ski doing donuts fifty feet from your boat. \n\nBut yeah, no, my heart didn't stop, and my brain was getting plenty of oxygen as far as I know. Just... just that washing machine feeling in my chest.\n\nDoctor: I want to make sure I understand the heart event clearly. When you were having that chest problem and they brought you to the hospital, did you ever lose consciousness or black out at any point—even for just a few seconds—before, during, or right after the ambulance ride?\n\nPatient: No, no, I never blacked out or lost consciousness or anything like that. Not even for a second. I was wide awake the whole time, watching the whole circus happen. Like I said, I remember the ambulance ride, I remember the squeaky cart, all of it. \n\nI actually remember looking out the back window of the ambulance and seeing Mrs. Gable's house as we went past. She lives on the corner of Elm and Maple. She's got these huge hydrangeas in her front yard, beautiful blue ones. She told my wife her secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil to make it acidic. We tried it last spring, saved all our Folgers grounds in a plastic tub under the sink. But our dog, Buster—he's a beagle mix, nose gets him into all sorts of trouble—he got into the tub and ate half the coffee grounds. I had to call the emergency vet at ten o'clock at night. Cost me two hundred dollars just for them to tell me he was gonna be jittery for a day and to make sure he drank water. He was practically vibrating, running laps around the coffee table until 3 AM. \n\nBut no, I didn't pass out or black out at all with the heart thing. I was awake for the whole ordeal.\n\nDoctor: When you had that cardiac scare and went to the hospital, did the doctors ever tell you that your heart had stopped beating or that you had gone into cardiac arrest—where your heart completely quit working for a while?\n\nPatient: Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a bit here! No, they never said cardiac arrest. It didn't stop beating, and it definitely didn't quit working. If my heart completely quit working, I'm pretty sure I wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you right now. \n\nBut you know, hearing the word arrest... it reminds me, my nephew Tommy almost got arrested last week. Well, not arrested, just a speeding ticket, but the boy acted like he was headed for the state pen. Got pulled over on Route 9 doing sixty in a forty-five zone. It was a state trooper, too. You know the ones with those wide-brimmed hats? They do not mess around. Tommy actually tried to tell the guy his speedometer was broken. I said, Tommy, you don't tell a cop your car is broken, they'll just write you another ticket for that! Kids these days, they think they can talk their way out of anything. \n\nBack when I was his age, if you got caught speeding, the cop would just follow you home and tell your dad. Took me three whole weekends, and I got paint in my hair that wouldn't wash out for a month. Looked like I had a weird gray stripe right down the middle of my head. \n\nBut anyway, to answer your question again, no. No cardiac arrest, the heart never stopped beating. I was sitting there idling for twenty minutes just watching this guy in a hard hat lean on a shovel... but anyway, no, no strokes or diabetes or anything like that. Just the heart scare.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned these memory problems started about a year and two months ago after your heart scare. Do your memory and thinking problems stay pretty much the same from day to day, or do they get noticeably better or worse at different times?\n\nPatient: You know, I haven't really paid attention to whether it's worse on some days than others. Honestly, since I retired, the days just kind of blend together anyway. It's hard to keep track of what day it even is unless it's a Tuesday, because that's trash day. \n\nAnd let me tell you, the city just switched over to those new automated garbage trucks a few months ago, right? So they gave everybody on the block these massive green bins. They're heavy, they're incredibly awkward to drag down the driveway, and half the time the mechanical arm on the truck knocks the lid completely off into the street anyway! I had to go out there in my slippers last week just to chase my lid down before the wind blew it into Mrs. Gable's yard. She’s already mad at me because my big oak tree drops acorns on her driveway, which, frankly, is just what trees do. You can't control nature. I told her, I said, \"Martha, if I could tell the tree where to drop 'em, I would.\" But she just scowled at me. She's had a chip on her shoulder ever since her cat ran away in 2019. \n\nBut anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, if my memory changes from day to day. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I haven't noticed any kind of pattern to it. It just feels like I'm always kind of scattered lately, no matter what day it is.\n\nDoctor: Looking back over this past year and two months since your heart scare, would you say your memory and thinking problems have been getting gradually worse, staying about the same, or have they actually improved at all?\n\nPatient: Getting worse... you know, a year and two months, that puts the heart thing right around Halloween, I think? Yeah, because we had just bought those massive bags of candy from Costco. My wife always insists on buying the name-brand chocolate because she doesn't want us to be \"that house\" on the block. You know the ones, they hand out those weird little peanut butter taffy things wrapped in the plain orange and black paper? Nobody even likes those! I swear they just recycle the same batch from 1975 every year. \n\nI actually broke a crown on one of those back when I was still working at the plant. Had to go to Dr. Miller—terrible dentist, by the way, real heavy hands. He retired a few years ago and moved down to Florida. Boca, I think. Or maybe Sarasota. I don't know how anybody stands the humidity down there, honestly. My brother-in-law went down there for a golf trip last summer and came back with a sunburn so bad he couldn't put a real shirt on for three days. He was walking around the house in this shiny silk robe looking like Hugh Hefner, it was ridiculous... \n\nBut, wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, if the memory is getting worse. No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I talk plenty, you can probably tell that. My wife says I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. She actually bought one of those monkeys once, at a flea market up near the lake. We used to go up there every summer, rent this little cabin. It didn't have AC, just these flimsy screen doors that let all the mosquitoes in. I spent half the vacation swatting at bugs with a rolled-up newspaper. Now I just look out the window at Mrs. Gable's yard. \n\nBut no, I don't get confused about where I am or anything like that. I know I'm right here in the clinic, and it's... well, it's daytime. Half the stores are boarded up. It's depressing, really. Used to be the place to go on a Saturday afternoon. But yeah, no problems with words or knowing where I am. Just the memory stuff.\n\nDoctor: When you had that cardiac scare about a year ago, did you lose consciousness at any point, or did you pass out? And did the doctors tell you that your heart stopped or that you weren't getting enough oxygen to your brain?\n\nPatient: Lose consciousness? Pass out? No, I don't think so. Good grief, they had that thing blaring the whole way to the hospital, and we only live about two miles away. \n\nI kept trying to tell the guy in the back with me—young kid, couldn't have been a day over twenty, barely had a mustache—I said, \"Son, you don't need the siren, there's no traffic on Elm Street at 10 AM on a Thursday.\" But he just ignored me and kept checking my blood pressure. They always pump those cuffs up way too tight, don't they? It feels like they're trying to pop your arm right off. I had a bruise shaped like a crescent moon for a week after that. They turned the theater into a rock climbing gym, if you can believe that. People paying good money to hang off plastic rocks indoors when there's a whole mountain range two hours away. No, nothing like that. No seizures or jerking around. I was perfectly still. Well, as still as you can be when you're strapped to a stretcher, anyway, but no, my body wasn't doing anything weird. 

Although, you know what does jerk around like crazy? Our washing machine. My wife overloaded it with heavy bath towels just the other day. I keep telling her, you can't just throw all the heavy stuff in on one side of the agitator, it throws the whole drum out of whack. It got to the spin cycle and sounded like a helicopter was landing in our laundry room. Bang, bang, bang! The whole machine actually walked itself about three inches across the linoleum. I had to get back there with a pry bar just to shimmy the darn thing back into place. 

They really don't make appliances like they used to, do they? My mother had this old Maytag when I was growing up, thing must have lasted thirty years. Thirty years! Now you buy a machine, it's got a computer board in it, it connects to the Wi-Fi... why on earth does a washing machine need Wi-Fi? Is it going to send me an email when my socks are clean? It's just more parts that can break, if you ask me. You pay a thousand dollars for a machine and you're lucky if it lasts five years before the motherboard fries. 

But anyway, no, no convulsions or shaking for me. Just my poor washing machine.

You'd think with all the taxes we pay, they could fix a pothole in under a decade, but no. Just the heart scare.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned these memory problems started about a year and two months ago after your heart scare. Honestly, since I retired, the days just kind of blend together anyway. It's hard to keep track of what day it even is unless it's a Tuesday, because that's trash day. \n\nAnd let me tell you, the city just switched over to those new automated garbage trucks a few months ago, right? So they gave everybody on the block these massive green bins. They're heavy, they're incredibly awkward to drag down the driveway, and half the time the mechanical arm on the truck knocks the lid completely off into the street anyway! My wife made me go to Sears to look at new ones, but Sears is closed now, isn't it? We ended up at Home Depot. They cost an arm and a leg, and the light they give off is so... sterile, you know? Like a hospital room. I miss the warm glow of the old bulbs. I actually bought a whole case of them at a garage sale a few years back, just to have them on hand. \n\nBut no, to answer your question, she never said I stopped responding to her.
